newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Manila peso move cheers business but not bankers.
newsitem.headline: Manila peso move cheers business but not bankers.

text.p: The Philippines' effective devaluation of the peso on Friday won the Central Bank few friends in the banking community with many bankers saying it had lost its credibility.
But businessmen welcomed the move saying it was bowing to the inevitable and that peso-defending high interest rates were no longer tenable.
In early morning trade the peso tumbled just over 11.5 percent to 29.45 to the dollar after the Central Bank announced it would allow the peso-dollar rate to move in a wider range.
"They (the authorities) were very consistent in that they agreed to allow the peso to weaken on a gradual but orderly basis," said Bank of America head of treasury in Manila, Jaime Panganiban.
"Today they destroyed that credibility. This will really be a big setback for this market in the eyes of the world."
"The abruptness is something unwelcome," Banco Santander treasurer Antonio Agcaoili said.

"This is basically a de facto devaluation. There's no way we can assess right away what the long-term impact will be. There's a lot of corporations (with foreign currency loans)...definitely it will have a corresponding impact on inflation," he added.
One banker estimated that Philippine companies could have up to $5 billion in oustanding foreign currency loans which they have to pay off with a now cheaper peso.
But president of the Philippines Federation of Industries, Raul Concepcion, said he was pleased with the change, saying that high interest rates to defend the peso were hurting business.

"We're pleased that the central bank has decided to allow free market forces to come in...they couln't continue to defend with high interest rates because loans to commercial banks jumped from 13 to 21 percent.
"If this were to continue the penalty to industry of higher interest rates would certainly be far greater than keeping the exchange rate at 26.40," he told Reuters Financial Television.
"So...this move is good in the sense we will go more on market-determined forces," he added.
Gavin Gunning, associate director of financial institution ratings with Standard & Poor's, said that banks could face higher risks from customers with foreign-currency obligations.
But offsetting that will be lower domestic interest rates, he said.
